summary: A published risk history beside a world that contradicts it. Two marketplace listings for the same machine cost the same and are five minutes of provisioning from running the same 2GB image. ask-a-clean-record's provider has measured it and never seen it refuse a start; ask-b-bad-record's says it refuses two starts in five. The Run takes the clean one, because the histories are recorded and priced nowhere so the placement falls through to the offer ID, and then that machine refuses the launch. Mercator strikes it out of the next placement and the Run runs on the listing whose provider published the worse record. Two claims live here. The world can make a machine refuse a start, so the redo an expected-redo-cost term would predict is an event a Blueprint can produce and a fixture can be falsified against, which is what a published rate with no producible consequence anywhere could never be. And a rate is what its provider measured and never what this world did: both decisions record both histories unchanged, so the refusal that really happened moves neither, because Mercator publishes nothing about machines on its providers' behalf.
